newsitem.title: USA: U.S. first-quarter economic growth highest in 9 years.
newsitem.headline: U.S. first-quarter economic growth highest in 9 years.

text.p: Stronger overseas sales and brisk production for inventories pushed the economy ahead at its fastest clip in more than nine years during the first quarter, the Commerce Department said on Friday.

The department revised upward its estimate of growth in gross domestic product to a booming 5.8 percent annual rate in the three months from January through March from the already-strong 5.6 percent rate it published a month ago.

It was the strongest quarterly expansion since a 6 percent rate of growth registered in the fourth quarter of 1987 and was well ahead of the 3.8 percent rate of GDP increase posted in last year's closing quarter.
The revised figure for first-quarter GDP growth was slightly below Wall Street economists' forecasts that it would advance at a 6 percent rate.
However, most analysts said they were not surprised by the figures. Many think the economy peaked in the first quarter and is headed for more subdued growth in the rest of the year.

"It was not much of a revision and, in essence, a yawner," Michael Niemira, an economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd, said. "Basically, the story line is there, it doesn't change anything looking forward. All the changes seem to be small."
"Nothing here changes anyone's view of anything," Joshua Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust, said.
"The first quarter was very, very strong. I expect the second quarter to slow down, but there's still a lot of underlying strength in the economy," he added.

"The upward revision to real GDP in the first quarter reflects upward revisions to inventory investment and to exports that more than offset downward revisions to consumer spending," the Commerce Department said.
A final estimate of GDP's first-quarter performance will be issued a month from now.

The revised report also included the first look at corporate profits during the opening months of 1997. After-tax profits surged $18.3 billion to $426.5 billion annual rate in the first quarter after a much smaller $6 billion increase in the final quarter last year.
GDP measures the value of all goods and services produced by workers and capital within a nation's borders and is the broadest measure of total economic activity.

Most analysts predict the pace of expansion in national output will slow to a rate around 2.5 percent a year during the current second quarter as consumer spending throttles back and industrial ouput levels off in response.
It was unclear, however, whether the anticipated slowdown would be enough to persuade Federal Reserve policymakers to once again hold off on interest-rate rises in July, as it did in May.

"What we knew before, we still know. We're looking for real GDP to grow between 1.5 percent and 2.0 percent in the second quarter," Ram Bhagavatula, chief financial economist at Citicorp Global Finance, said.
"As far as Fed policy is concerned, the Fed is paying close attention to demand volatility. Retail sales were weak in April. We'll see what May and June brings."

Commerce said its revised estimates showed that businesses boosted their inventories at the fastest rate in two years during the first quarter, up $51.4 billion instead of the $46.1 billion estimated a month ago.
That was the strongest pace of restocking since the first quarter of 1995, when inventories were being added to at a $53.7 billion annual rate.
While inventory-building bolsters the economy in the period in which it occurs, it generally foreshadows slower GDP growth ahead because business strives to keep production in line with sales.
Trade also stimulated the economy more than initially thought, as exports increased at at a $23.1 billion rate in the first quarter instead of the $17 billion rate Commerce reported last month.

But personal consumption spending -- the fuel for about two-thirds of national economic activity -- was not quite as robust as estimated a month ago. Spending advanced at a $66.2 billion rate rather than $73.5 billion, Commerce said.

Real final sales -- a measure of GDP that subtracts changes in business inventories and that is closely tracked by economists as an indicator of demand -- was revised down to a 3.8 percent increase from last month's estimated 3.9 percent and from a 4.9 percent advance in the fourth quarter last year.
Inflation remained relatively muted, according to two measures of price rises in the GDP report, though not as tame as during last year's closing quarter.

The implicit price deflator advanced at a 2.2 percent annual rate in the first quarter instead of the 2.3 percent estimated last month. But that was up from a 1.5 percent fourth-quarter increase last year.

The fixed-weights measure of price changes rose at a 2.8 percent rate, rather than 2.7 percent, well ahead of the fourth quarter's 1.9 percent advance and the largest for any quarter since a 3.3 percent rise in the first quarter of 1995.
